items.stem: Which is the definition of electromotive force?
options: Energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge
Energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge
items.answer: Energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge
items.markingKey: e.m.f. = W/Q for a source.

items.stem: Explain why the headlights of a car dim when the starter motor is operated.
items.answer: The starter motor draws a very large current; the lost volts Ir across the battery's internal resistance increase, so the terminal p.d. across the headlights falls.
items.markingKey: large current [1]; larger Ir so terminal p.d. falls [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a high-voltage power supply is designed with a very large internal resistance.
items.answer: If the terminals are short-circuited (e.g. by a person), the large internal resistance limits the current to a safe value.
items.markingKey: limits current on short circuit [1]; safety [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 4.5 V and internal resistance 1.5 Ω is connected to a 5.0 Ω resistor. Determine the current in the circuit.
items.markingKey: I = E/(R + r) = 4.5/(5.0 + 1.5) = 0.692 A. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 3.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 10 Ω resistor. Calculate the current, the terminal p.d. and the power wasted inside the source.

A 6.0 V battery with internal resistance 1.5 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. (a) Define e.m.f. (b) Calculate the terminal p.d. (c) Explain why the battery becomes warm. (d) Calculate the maximum current the battery could supply.
items.answer: (a) Energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge passing through the source. (b) 4.36 V (c) Energy is transferred to thermal energy in the internal resistance (I²r). (d) 4.0 A
items.markingKey: (a) Energy transferred from other forms to electrical energy per unit charge passing through the source [1] (b) V = E − Ir: 4.36 V [1] (c) Energy is transferred to thermal energy in the internal resistance (I²r) [1] (d) short circuit E/r: 4.0 A [1]

items.stem: A cell of e.m.f. 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 2.5 Ω resistor. What is the current?
Describe how to determine the e.m.f. and internal resistance of a cell using a graph.
items.answer: Measure terminal p.d. V and current I for several external resistances; plot V against I; e.m.f. = y-intercept; internal resistance = −gradient.
items.markingKey: measure V and I for varying R [1]; V vs I graph [1]; E = intercept, r = −gradient [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why a voltmeter connected directly across a cell reads very nearly its e.m.f.
items.answer: A voltmeter has a very high resistance so the current is almost zero; the lost volts Ir are negligible.
items.markingKey: very small current [1]; Ir negligible [1] [2]

items.stem: Derive the formula for the combined resistance of two resistors in series using Kirchhoff's laws.
items.answer: Same current I in each (first law); V = V₁ + V₂ (second law) so IR = IR₁ + IR₂, giving R = R₁ + R₂.
items.markingKey: same current [1]; p.d.s add, divide by I [1] [2]

items.stem: Derive the formula for the combined resistance of two resistors in parallel using Kirchhoff's laws.
items.answer: Same p.d. V across each; I = I₁ + I₂ (first law), so V/R = V/R₁ + V/R₂, giving 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂.
items.markingKey: same p.d. [1]; currents add, divide by V [1] [2]

Explain why the combined resistance of resistors in parallel is less than the smallest resistance.
items.answer: Adding another path increases the total current for the same p.d., so the total resistance decreases below that of any single branch.

items.stem: Explain how Kirchhoff's first law follows from conservation of charge.
items.answer: Charge cannot build up at a junction, so the charge flowing in per second equals the charge flowing out per second.
items.markingKey: no accumulation [1]; rate in = rate out [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf calculates the combined resistance of 4.0 Ω and 12 Ω in parallel as 1/4.0 + 1/12 = 0.333 Ω. Identify the error, give the correct value, and explain how Yusuf could have checked the answer.

items.stem: A 12 V supply is connected across resistors of 2.0 kΩ and 4.0 kΩ in series. What is the p.d. across the 4.0 kΩ resistor?
Explain how a potential divider containing an LDR can be used to switch on a street lamp when it gets dark.
items.answer: In the dark the LDR resistance increases, so the p.d. across it rises; if the output is taken across the LDR, this larger p.d. triggers the switching circuit to turn on the lamp.

items.stem: Explain why a potentiometer measures the e.m.f. of a cell more accurately than a voltmeter.
items.answer: At balance no current flows from the cell, so there are no lost volts across its internal resistance; a voltmeter draws a small current and reads slightly less than the e.m.f.
items.markingKey: no current at balance [1]; voltmeter draws current / lost volts [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a high-voltage power supply is designed with a very large internal resistance. (b) Explain why the headlights of a car dim when the starter motor is operated.
items.answer: (a) If the terminals are short-circuited (e.g. by a person), the large internal resistance limits the current to a safe value. (b) The starter motor draws a very large current; the lost volts Ir across the battery's internal resistance increase, so the terminal p.d. across the headlights falls.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the combined resistance of resistors in parallel is less than the smallest resistance. (b) Explain how Kirchhoff's first law follows from conservation of charge.
items.answer: (a) Adding another path increases the total current for the same p.d., so the total resistance decreases below that of any single branch. (b) Charge cannot build up at a junction, so the charge flowing in per second equals the charge flowing out per second.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why connecting a voltmeter of low resistance across the output of a potential divider changes the output p.d. (b) Explain how a potential divider containing an LDR can be used to switch on a street lamp when it gets dark.
items.answer: (a) The voltmeter in parallel with the output resistor reduces the combined resistance of that section, so it takes a smaller share of the supply p.d. (b) In the dark the LDR resistance increases, so the p.d. across it rises; if the output is taken across the LDR, this larger p.d. triggers the switching circuit to turn on the lamp.
items.markingKey: (a) parallel combination lower resistance [1]; output p.d. decreases [1] [2] (b) LDR resistance rises in dark [1]; larger share of p.d. across LDR [1]; output across LDR triggers switch [1] [3]
